blocks.text: But if one compares Rashi on that biblical passage, then either סום must be emended to עגור in our Rashi passage on the Talmud, or in that Rashi passage on the Bible the order must be שפנונא וסנונית וכורכיא; in any case כרוכיא is the crane and not, as Landau (Aruch s.v. קליאם) would have it, the raven. Landau lets himself be misled by the similarity of sound with the Greek Κόραξ [Korax]*); but the word far rather deserves to be compared with the Arabic كُرْكِيْ [kurkī], by which Saadias renders עגור at Jerem. l. c., and which in that language denotes the crane.
The remarkable structure of this bird's windpipe enables it to produce a piercing, loud cry, to which our Talmud passage alludes. See Voigt l. c. 2. p. 355.

Chulin 63a it says: אנפה is a cruel, high-flying bird, the actual דיה רגונית (cruel דיה, see article Stork), but it is called אנפה because it is angry with its companions (אנף, whence the noun אף, anger), i.e., it fights and bites with them and is fierce. [p. 170]

Rashi cites this Talmud passage on Lev. 11, 19*) and adds: וכדומה לי שקוראין אותו איירון "and as I believe, it is the bird that is called Héron". Indeed the heron has a fierce nature; it is wild and given to biting (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 359). Even when it is shot lame, it defends itself furiously against the dogs and aims the thrusts of its beak at their heads, which is why one never sets a dog loose on it (Beumer: Populäre Naturgesch. p. 197). It has the same stilt-legs as the stork, with which it has much resemblance in general, and so it is rightly mentioned in Scripture next to that bird.
Chulin 63a it says: The bird אריכי שקי וירוקי, which has long legs (i.e. stilt-legs) and is ירוק in colour, may not be eaten.

As is well known, ירוק can mean green, yellow and blue (see Ture Sahab on Jore Dea §. 38, 1, and Isserels ibid. §. 188, 1). The night heron (Ardea Nycticorax) unites all these colours in itself. Head, back and shoulders are black, steel-blue and with a greenish shimmer; in the old male the belly is sulphur-yellow. It has stilt-legs and is rightly forbidden, since among the heron family the heron (§. 200) is expressly forbidden by Scripture.

Chulin 63a it says: The bird שקיטנא with long and red legs is permitted to be eaten. As proof (וסמנך) serves the מורומא. On this Rashi: There are two kinds of the bird שקיטנא; the one that has long legs (stilt-legs) and is red in body may be eaten, for as proof serves the bird מורומא, which is similarly shaped and generally known as clean. Aruch explains this latter word itself as a Persian one, by which every red and at the same time long object is designated. We are to take שקיטנא and מורומא here as identical and merely as provincialisms;

[p. 171] both names denote the first kind of flamingo, Phoenicopterus ruber. It is purple-red with an elongated neck and legs. Stretched out, its length amounts to 6 feet. It was probably considered clean because, owing to the webbing on its feet, it was counted among the family of water birds rather than that of the stilt birds. On the second kind mentioned above see the following article.

Chulin 63a it is said that the common flamingo (שקימנא, §. 202) is permitted to be eaten, whereas the נוצי וסומקי (short and red) is forbidden to be eaten; the lesser flamingo, Phoenicopterus minor, lives in southern Africa and is smaller than the former (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 368). That the different kinds of one and the same bird family differed in ritual respect need not cause surprise, since in this matter the different regions did not always follow the same usage, cf. §. 186 on the owl, §. 210 on the starling, and §. 219 on the moorhen. Yet a distinction was also made, without any reason being given more precisely, among the kinds themselves, as with the parrot (§. 185) and with our bird.

Chulin 63a it is said: The חסידה is the דיה לבנה (white Daja), but it is called חסידה (the pious one) because it lovingly shares its food with its companions.*). That חסידה is the stork cannot be doubted. Rashi translates the word (Lev. 11, 19) by צינניה, Cigogne. The only question is how the Talmud could call the stork דיה לבנה, "white vulture"? One should note, however, that דיה, or דיו (B. mez. 24b, cf. above §. 196) denotes only the black or the common vulture; the notion [p. 172] of the name lies in the root word ראה, to hover, to fly high, and so by a more specific qualifying addition that notion can also be transferred to other high-flying birds of prey. The stork, which on the whole is white and black only on the wing-feathers, can rightly be called ריה לבנה "the white high-flying bird", while the heron (§. 200) on account of its fierceness is called ריה רגונית "the cruel high-hovering bird". The two names of the stork are thus not an identity of essence but a mere identity of name, in the sense: one can call the stork the white vulture, which itself, on account of its lofty flight, is called ריה κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν [kat᾽ exochēn]. —

The name ריה לבנה corresponds perfectly to ריה חיורתא, whose gall possesses healing power against the poison of the scorpion's sting (Ketuboth 50a). Here Rashi translates the name by וושטול, evidently corrupt for ולטור, as ריו on B. mez. 24b; but also substantially incorrect, since here only the stork can be meant.

Pliny (h. n. 29, 5, 33) says of the stork: Contra venena omnia cicouiarum ventriculus valet. "Against all poison the stomach of storks helps"; Harduin on the passage says that the inner lining of the stomach is meant here; that healing power against poisons was thus known early.

Finally it may be noted that the love (חסר) attributed to the stork is also related by Aristotle (l. c. 9, 14, 1). He says: Well known is the tale about the storks, namely that the old ones are in turn fed by their young.
